title: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters
learningObjectives: Manage entrapment and prevent death at release in crush syndrome.
Recognize and respond to crowd crush and mass-gathering hazards.
Apply hazard-specific tactics for transport crashes and natural disasters.
Protect vulnerable populations: children, elderly, technology-dependent patients.

summary.title: Structural Collapse & Crush Syndrome
summary.content: Don't enter unstable structures — USAR teams shore, breach, and perform confined-space rescue; EMS supports them and may treat in voids only when it's declared safe. Crush syndrome follows prolonged compression of large muscle masses (classically hours, but sooner with heavy loads): at RELEASE, potassium, acid, and myoglobin flood the circulation → arrhythmia/cardiac arrest ('smiling death') and later kidney failure. Before release: IV/IO normal saline (~1–1.5 L/h adult; avoid potassium-containing fluids), cardiac monitor, prepare for hyperkalemia (calcium, sodium bicarbonate, nebulized albuterol per protocol). If no access and release can't wait, some protocols allow a tourniquet on the limb before release as a last resort.

summary.title: Crowd Crush & Mass Gatherings
summary.content: Danger starts when crowd density exceeds ~4–5 people per m² and people can no longer move independently; crowd 'waves' and surges precede collapse. Victims die standing — compressive (traumatic) asphyxia — not mainly from trampling. Signs: facial/neck plethora and petechiae, subconjunctival hemorrhage, hypoxia. Actions: alert event control to stop inflow and open exits, extract from the edges, open airway, O2, ventilate, triage normally. Pre-plan mass gatherings: medical posts, access/egress lanes, heat/cold plans, intoxication, communications with event security.

summary.title: Transportation Incidents
summary.content: Closed incidents with a manifest — get the passenger count early and account for everyone (including those ejected or wandered off). BUS/COACH: rollover = multi-system blunt trauma, entrapment, fuel. RAIL: isolate power (overhead lines, third rail) before entry; long extrication; hazmat cargo. AIRCRAFT: approach upwind, fuel fires, composite fiber hazards (respiratory protection), wide debris field; airport emergency plans. MARITIME: drowning, hypothermia, staged shore triage.

summary.title: Natural Disaster Tactics
summary.content: EARTHQUAKE: aftershocks — stay out of damaged buildings; crush and fractures; compound incident (hospitals damaged). FLOOD: never enter moving water — ~6 inches (15 cm) can knock you down and ~1 foot (30 cm) can float most cars; electrocution, contaminated water, hypothermia; swift-water teams only. HEAT WAVE: exertional or classic heat stroke = cool FIRST (cold-water immersion is best), transport second. WINTER STORM: hypothermia, CO from heaters/generators, falls. HURRICANE: pre-landfall evacuation of dependent patients; post-storm CO, chainsaw injuries, missed dialysis. WILDFIRE: protect your exit route; burns, smoke, CO/cyanide.

summary.title: Vulnerable Populations
summary.content: CHILDREN: JumpSTART triage; keep with caregivers where possible; document and protect UNACCOMPANIED MINORS (photo, tag, safe supervised area) — never release to unverified adults; smaller airways and higher surface area → faster hypothermia and toxin absorption. ELDERLY: atypical presentations, falls, medication dependence, heat vulnerability. TECHNOLOGY-DEPENDENT: home ventilators, O2 concentrators, dialysis, insulin — power outages create patients. DISABILITIES: service animals stay with owners; communication aids; evacuation chairs. PREGNANCY: left lateral tilt; fetal well-being depends on maternal oxygenation and perfusion.

clinicalPearls: Fluids before freedom: start IV saline before releasing a crush victim.
Peaked T waves after extrication = hyperkalemia → calcium now.
Crowd crush kills by asphyxia — the fix is releasing the chest and ventilating.
Turn around, don't drown: no rescuer enters moving water without swift-water training and gear.
Unaccompanied children get a name, a photo, a tag, and a guardian-in-charge — reunification is a safety process.
redFlags: Releasing a long-entrapped limb without fluids or a monitor.
Crowd surges, people unable to raise their arms, screams from one area of a crowd.
Power outage calls for ventilator/O2-dependent patients — rising heat or cold.
commonMistakes: Using lactated Ringer's (contains potassium) for crush pre-release fluids.
Releasing unaccompanied children to any adult who claims them.
Treating heat stroke without aggressive cooling on scene.
Forgetting to request the passenger manifest in transport incidents.
memoryAids: Crush: 'Fluids before freedom; calcium for the K.'
Flood: '6 inches knocks you down, 1 foot floats your car.'

decisionTrees.title: Crush Victim Release
decisionTrees.content:
Entrapped > ~1 h (large muscle mass) or heavy compression?
  → YES: crush syndrome risk
     → IV/IO access → NS 1–1.5 L/h BEFORE release (no K+ fluids)
     → Cardiac monitor; prepare calcium, bicarbonate, albuterol per protocol
     → No IV & release can't wait → consider TQ before release (protocol/last resort)
     → Release → watch for hyperkalemia (peaked T, wide QRS, arrhythmia)
  → NO: standard trauma care

references: International Society of Nephrology / Renal Disaster Relief Task Force crush syndrome recommendations
US National Weather Service 'Turn Around Don't Drown'
AAP / ASPR pediatric disaster and family reunification guidance
